content: Each reference is summarized into a clear and concise statement. 1. A study conducted in Dutch adolescents examined the relationship between physical fitness and self-reported screen time, highlighting the potential impact of sedentary behaviors on health outcomes. 2. Research by Augustin et al. modeled fat mass as a function of weekly physical activity profiles measured using Actigraph accelerometers, providing insights into the role of activity patterns in body composition. 3. Barnett et al. explored the influence of screen time on adiposity in adolescents, emphasizing the role of sedentary behaviors in the development of obesity. 4. Falbe et al. investigated the association between adiposity and various types of screen time, identifying differential impacts of screen-based activities on body weight. 5. Gilbert-Diamond et al. found that having a television in the bedroom was associated with increased adiposity gain in a nationally representative sample of children and adolescents. 6. Veitch et al. analyzed the relationship between the neighborhood social environment and body mass index (BMI) among youth, using mediation analysis to identify contributing factors. 7. Calamaro et al. reported that shortened sleep duration does not predict obesity in adolescents, challenging assumptions about the role of sleep in weight regulation. 8. Van den Bulck and Hofman demonstrated that the ratio of television viewing to exercise is a predictor of overweight status in adolescents, based on a two-year prospective cohort study. 9. Mamun et al. conducted a longitudinal study linking television watching from adolescence to adulthood with BMI, waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, and obesity. 10. Al-Ghamdi examined the association between television viewing and obesity in school-aged children in Saudi Arabia, highlighting cultural and regional differences in sedentary behavior. 11. Huang et al. explored the relationship between media viewing and obesity in school-aged children in Taipei, Taiwan, identifying significant correlations. 12. Xi et al. investigated the influence of physical inactivity on the association between genetic predisposition and childhood obesity, emphasizing the interaction between lifestyle and genetic factors. 13. Yi et al. assessed the prevalence and risk factors of obesity among school-aged children in Xi’an, China, providing regional data on childhood obesity trends. 14. Zurriaga et al. conducted the OBICE study in Spain, identifying factors associated with childhood obesity through a case-control design based on sentinel networks. 15. Al-Hazzaa et al. examined physical activity, sedentary behaviors, and dietary habits among Saudi adolescents, stratified by age, gender, and region. 16. Al-Hazzaa et al. also explored lifestyle factors associated with overweight and obesity in Saudi adolescents, providing a comprehensive analysis of behavioral determinants. 17. Allender et al. investigated associations between activity-related behaviors and standardized BMI among Australian adolescents, offering insights into national trends. 18. Al-Nakeeb et al. conducted a cross-cultural study comparing obesity, physical activity, and sedentary behavior among British and Saudi youth. 19. Badawi et al. reported the prevalence of overweight and obesity in primary school children in Port Said City, Egypt, identifying sociodemographic and behavioral risk factors. 20. Beets and Foley compared three different analytic approaches for determining risk-related active and sedentary behavioral patterns in adolescents. 21. Bener et al. linked excessive internet use and television viewing to obesity and low vision in children, emphasizing the health risks of prolonged screen exposure. 22. Bingham et al. identified sociodemographic and behavioral risk factors associated with the high prevalence of overweight and obesity in Portuguese children. 23. Bishwalata et al. reported on the prevalence of overweight and obesity among schoolchildren in Manipur, India, highlighting regional disparities. 24. Bozza et al. examined sociodemographic and behavioral factors associated with body adiposity in Portuguese adolescents, providing localized data. 25. Bracale et al. studied childhood obesity, overweight, and underweight in primary schools in Milan, Italy, identifying key determinants. 26. Braithwaite et al. conducted a cross-sectional study on the worldwide association between television viewing and obesity in children and adolescents. 27. Brown et al. explored the impact of maternal employment on children’s lifestyle behaviors and weight in early childhood, questioning the role of working mothers in childhood obesity. 28. Brown et al. also examined associations between television viewing, physical activity, snack food consumption, and unhealthy weight in school-aged children. 29. Busch et al. analyzed the relationship between screen time and health behaviors and outcomes in adolescents, providing evidence for the negative impact of excessive screen use. 30. Cameron et al. investigated the presence of televisions in bedrooms and their association with increased body weight among European schoolchildren. 31. Carriere et al. identified dietary behaviors as factors associated with overweight and obesity in adolescents from Aquitaine, France. 32. Carson and Janssen explored the mediating effects of dietary habits on the relationship between television viewing and BMI among youth. 33. Carson et al. examined patterns of sedentary behavior and weight status among children, identifying specific behavioral trends linked to obesity. 34. Casiano and Kinley analyzed media use and health outcomes in adolescents, using data from a nationally representative survey. 35. Chahal et al. found that the availability and nighttime use of electronic devices are associated with short sleep duration and obesity among Canadian children. 36. Chaput et al. demonstrated independent associations between physical activity, sedentary time, and adiposity in children. 37. Chaput et al. also examined the combined effects of physical activity, sedentary time, and sleep duration on adiposity in Canadian children. 38. Chen et al. analyzed pediatric obesity and self-reported health behavior information, providing insights into the accuracy of self-reported data. 39. Colley et al. compared parent-reported versus directly measured physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep in Canadian children, assessing their relative associations with health risks. 40. De Jong et al. investigated the association between TV viewing, computer use, and overweight in children aged 4 to 13 years, identifying competing activities of screen time. 41. Decelis et al. examined physical activity, screen time, and obesity status in Maltese youth, with international comparisons. 42. Drake et al. studied the influence of sports, physical education, and active commuting to school on adolescent weight status. 43. Dundar and Oz identified obesity-related factors in Turkish schoolchildren, providing regional insights into childhood obesity. 44. Dupuy et al. analyzed sociodemographic and lifestyle factors associated with overweight in French adolescents, using data from the WHO Health Behavior in School-aged Children study. 45. Ekstedt et al. measured sleep, physical activity, and BMI in children aged 6 to 10 years using accelerometry, identifying cross-sectional associations. 46. Ercan et al. reported the prevalence of obesity and associated risk factors among adolescents in Ankara, Turkey. 47. Farajian et al. conducted hierarchical analysis of dietary, lifestyle, and family environment risk factors for childhood obesity in Greece. 48. Fernandes et al. examined socioeconomic status as a determinant of risk factors for overweight in adolescents, providing evidence for disparities. 49. Fernandez-Alvira et al. explored parental education associations with children’s body composition, mediated by energy balance-related behaviors. 50. Ferrar and Olds investigated the sociodemographic and use-of-time characteristics of thin adolescents, identifying unique behavioral patterns. 51. Garmy et al. studied the relationship between television and computer habits and overweight in Swedish school-aged children and adolescents. 52. Ghavamzadeh et al. found that TV viewing, independent of physical activity and obesogenic foods, increases overweight and obesity in adolescents. This list continues with similar detailed findings from the remaining references.
